title: Temperature is the average kinetic energy of molecules
summary: Compare two gases: the hotter one has faster molecules and a larger average kinetic energy.
alt: Two boxes of gas side by side, one at fixed temperature and one adjustable, with bars showing mean kinetic energy.

gas.label: Gas molecules
gas.text: The molecules of the gas (colour = speed: blue slow, red fast).

u.label: Mean kinetic energy
u.text: Average kinetic energy of one molecule.

shapes.text: average kinetic energy of a molecule
(KE ratio {{KEB|2}}; the speed ratio is its square root)

steps.title: Same temperature, same average energy
steps.text: Both gases are at 300 K. The molecules move in all directions at many different speeds, but the **average kinetic energy** is the same in both boxes.

steps.title: Heat B to 1200 K
steps.text: Heat gas B to four times the kelvin temperature. The molecules of B turn red and move **twice as fast**. Their average kinetic energy is **four times** bigger.

steps.title: Temperature ∝ average kinetic energy
steps.text: This is the meaning of temperature: \( \overline{KE} \propto T \). Kinetic energy goes with T; the speed goes with \( \sqrt{T} \).

steps.title: Cool B to near zero
steps.text: Cool gas B far below 300 K. The molecules slow down. At **absolute zero (0 K)** an ideal gas would have no motion at all.

steps.title: Try your own temperature
steps.text: Choose any temperature for B and compare the kinetic-energy bars and the speed ratio.

readouts.label: KE of B ÷ KE of A

formulas.title: Kinetic energy and temperature
formulas.text: For a gas molecule the average kinetic energy is proportional to the kelvin temperature.

formulas.title: Speed
formulas.text: Quadruple the temperature and the speed only doubles.

challenges.title: Now you try
challenges.prompt: Gas B is heated from 300 K to **1200 K**. How many times larger is the **average kinetic energy** of its molecules?
challenges.hint: KE is proportional to the kelvin temperature.

challenges.title: Now you try
challenges.prompt: Gas B is heated from 300 K to **1200 K**. By what factor does the **speed** of its molecules increase?
challenges.hint: Speed goes as the square root of T.

challenges.title: Now you try
challenges.prompt: What happens to the molecules of an ideal gas at **0 K**?
challenges.hint: Zero temperature = zero average kinetic energy.
challenges.explain: At absolute zero an ideal gas would have no kinetic energy: the molecules would be at rest.

takeaways: **Temperature measures the average kinetic energy** of the molecules: \( \overline{KE} \propto T \).
Speed goes as \( \sqrt{T} \): four times the kelvin temperature means twice the speed.
At absolute zero (0 K) ideal-gas molecules would have no motion.

notes.title: Connects to
notes.text: This is why heating a gas raises its **pressure** (faster molecules hit harder) and why **internal energy** of a gas depends on temperature.
